newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end sharply higher, weather cited.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end sharply higher, weather cited.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended sharply higher on Monday, led by new crop amid forecasts for another hot, dry spell in the U.S. Midwest, traders said.

Forecasts called for cooler temperatures through Thursday, followed by a hot, dry weekend. Long-range forecasts suggested the heat wave would linger through early next week with no substantial rainfall expected, meteorologists said.
August is considered the critical weather month for soybeans. A hot, dry start to that month could stress developing crops, traders said.
Soybeans ended 18 to 3-1/4 cents per bushel higher with November up 18 at $6.19-1/4.

Nearbys struggled with indications demand for old crop supplies was waning. Traders said end users were expecting a record large new crop and were willing to wait rather than pay a $1.50 per bushel premium for prompt shipment.

Meanwhile, demand for new crop supplies appeared to be on the rise as concerns mounted of weather-related yield losses in Asia, traders said. There was talk China was looking to buy 200,000 tonnes of U.S. new crop soybeans and Taiwan was seen tendering for at least one cargo.

"There's a mushrooming demand base under this market," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Iowa. "If some of these areas around the world continue to have (weather) problems, who knows what will happen to demand."
Another hot, dry week in China increased concerns of crop damage but Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said the corn crop had been hurt more than soybeans.

"These (soybean) crops tend to be more hearty and can withstand more abuse from heat and dryness," Davis said in his weather update. "However, they can only withstand so much and long-term dryness, lack of irrigation reserves, and periods of heat will significantly reduce yield potential.

USDA weekly export data also suggested buyers would switch to new crop. USDA on Monday said 843,149,000 bushels of soybeans had been inspected for export in the 1996-97 (Sept/Aug) year versus export sales of roughly 894 million.
The discrepancy suggested to some traders that world buyers were cancelling purchases or switching to new crop.

After the close of trading, USDA said 62 percent of the U.S. soybean crop was rated good to excellent, unchanged from the previous week. The trade had expected an improvement in crop ratings following last week's rains.

On the day, funds bought at least 14 million bushels of soybeans. Pit sources said Rosenthal Collins, SAK Futures, FIMAT Futures, E.D. and F. Man International, Refco Inc and Merrill Lynch each bought at least 1.5 million bushels November. Cargill Inc bought four million November and sold 3.5 million November.
In options, Lind-Waldock bought 550 November $7.50 calls at 6-1/2 cents and 550 September $7.50 calls at 3-1/4 to 3-1/2 cents, traders said.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 58,500 contracts, compared with Friday's actual volume of 33,978 contracts. Options volume was pegged at 17,000 contracts, against Friday's 8,546.
